intro.displayText: Welcome to C#, a language people use to build games, apps and the servers behind websites. Your mission today: make a welcome sign for the Grove that prints line by line.
intro.speechText: Welcome to C sharp, a language people use to build games, apps and the servers behind websites. Your mission today is to make a welcome sign for the Grove that prints line by line.

recap.displayText: You wrote your first C# program, and the sign prints perfectly! Your new word is statement: one instruction, and most of them end with a semicolon.
recap.speechText: You wrote your first C sharp program, and the sign prints perfectly! Your new word is statement, which means one instruction, and most of them end with a semicolon.

intro.displayText: C# runs a huge amount of real software, from ASP.NET Core web APIs to Unity games, and it's where this track is heading: your own backend. Unlike JavaScript, it's compiled, so the compiler checks the whole program before a single line runs. You'll learn how a C# program is put together and how to read compile errors. Then you'll get a launch checklist off the ground.
intro.speechText: C sharp runs a huge amount of real software, from web APIs to Unity games, and it's where this track is heading: your own backend. Unlike JavaScript, it's compiled, so the compiler checks the whole program before a single line runs. You'll learn how a C sharp program is put together and how to read compile errors. recap.displayText: Nice work: the checklist compiles and the output matches exactly. The gotcha: one compile error means none of the program runs, and one mistake can cause several errors, so always fix the first one first. Next, you'll store data in variables and meet C#'s types.
recap.speechText: Nice work. The checklist compiles and the output matches exactly. The gotcha is that one compile error means none of the program runs, and one mistake can cause several errors, so always fix the first one first. Next, you'll store data in variables and meet the types C sharp uses.

intro.displayText: Programs need to remember things, like a player's name or how many coins they have. Your mission: build a player card that keeps its facts in variables and prints them.
intro.speechText: Programs need to remember things, like a player's name or how many coins they have. Your mission is to build a player card that keeps its facts in variables and prints them.

recap.displayText: Your player card prints straight from its variables! Your new word is variable: a named box that holds a value you can change.
recap.speechText: Your player card prints straight from its variables! Your new word is variable, a named box that holds a value you can change.

intro.displayText: Every real program juggles data: prices, counts, names, flags. C# makes you choose a type for each one and holds you to it, which catches a whole family of bugs before the code ever runs. You'll meet the core types, var, constants and formatted string interpolation. Then you'll fix a road trip calculator the compiler refuses to build.
intro.speechText: Every real program juggles data, like prices, counts, names and flags. C sharp makes you choose a type for each one and holds you to it, which catches a whole family of bugs before the code ever runs. You'll meet the core types, var, constants and formatted string interpolation. Then you'll fix a road trip calculator the compiler refuses to build.

recap.displayText: The calculator compiles and every number checks out. The gotcha: an int divided by an int is an int, so 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. Make one side a double or decimal when you need the fraction. Next, your programs start making decisions with if and switch.
recap.speechText: The calculator compiles and every number checks out. The gotcha is that an int divided by an int is an int, so seven divided by two is three, not three and a half. Make one side a double or a decimal when you need the fraction. Next, your programs start making decisions with if and switch.

intro.displayText: Programs get clever when they can choose what to do. Your mission: run the Rocket Ride checker at the Grove Fair and decide who gets to ride.
intro.speechText: Programs get clever when they can choose what to do. Your mission is to run the Rocket Ride checker at the Grove Fair and decide who gets to ride.

recap.displayText: Your ride checker makes the right call for every rider! Your new word is condition: a true-or-false question that an if statement checks.
recap.speechText: Your ride checker makes the right call for every rider! Your new word is condition, a true or false question that an if statement checks.

intro.displayText: Almost every feature you'll build branches somewhere: pricing tiers, permissions, validation, error handling. C# gives you if and else for simple branches, and switch expressions with patterns for cleaner multi-way decisions. You'll also meet short-circuit logic, which real code relies on to avoid crashing on missing data. Then you'll write the pricing rules for a cinema.
intro.speechText: Almost every feature you'll build branches somewhere, like pricing tiers, permissions, validation and error handling. C sharp gives you if and else for simple branches, and switch expressions with patterns for cleaner multi way decisions. You'll also meet short circuit logic, which real code relies on to avoid crashing on missing data. Then you'll write the pricing rules for a cinema.

recap.displayText: The pricing rules hold up for every age and every day of the week. The gotcha: a switch expression tries its arms from top to bottom, so put the narrowest patterns first. Get the order wrong and C# reports the arm that can never match as an error. Next, you'll repeat work with loops over arrays and lists.
recap.speechText: The pricing rules hold up for every age and every day of the week. The gotcha is that a switch expression tries its arms from top to bottom, so put the narrowest patterns first. Get the order wrong and C sharp reports the arm that can never match as an error. Next, you'll repeat work with loops over arrays and lists.

intro.displayText: Treasure hunters have to keep track of lots of things at once. Your mission: list every treasure in the Grove's chest and add up what it's all worth.
intro.speechText: Treasure hunters have to keep track of lots of things at once. Your mission is to list every treasure in the Grove's chest and add up what it's all worth.

recap.displayText: Every treasure is listed, and the total adds up! Your new word is loop: code that repeats, once for each item or a set number of times.
recap.speechText: Every treasure is listed, and the total adds up! Your new word is loop, which means code that repeats, once for each item or a set number of times.

intro.displayText: Real programs rarely handle one value at a time, but orders, rows, messages and scores by the hundred. Arrays, lists and loops are how C# deals with collections, and off-by-one mistakes in them are among the most common bugs in any language. You'll meet both kinds of collection, every kind of loop, and the exceptions you get when you step outside one. Then you'll debug and finish a gradebook.
intro.speechText: Real programs rarely handle one value at a time, but orders, rows, messages and scores by the hundred. Arrays, lists and loops are how C sharp deals with collections, and off by one mistakes in them are among the most common bugs in any language. You'll meet both kinds of collection, every kind of loop, and the exceptions you get when you step outside one. Then you'll debug and finish a gradebook.

recap.displayText: The gradebook's numbers are right, even for an empty class. The gotcha: indexes run from 0 to Count - 1, so a loop condition with <= reads one past the end and throws. Next, you'll package code into your own methods, with parameters and return values.
recap.speechText: The gradebook's numbers are right, even for an empty class. The gotcha is that indexes run from zero to the count minus one, so a loop that keeps going while i is less than or equal to the count reads one past the end and throws. Next, you'll package code into your own methods, with parameters and return values.

intro.displayText: Methods let you give a job a name, then use it again and again. Your mission: write two spells for the Grove's spell book, one that shouts and one that doubles.
intro.speechText: Methods let you give a job a name, then use it again and again. Your mission is to write two spells for the Grove's spell book, one that shouts and one that doubles.

recap.displayText: Both spells work every time you call them! Your new word is parameter: a value you hand to a method when you call it.
recap.speechText: Both spells work every time you call them! Your new word is parameter, a value you hand to a method when you call it.

intro.displayText: Good code is mostly small methods with clear names, each doing one job you can test on its own. You'll write your own: parameters, return values, optional parameters, overloads, and the out parameters behind the TryParse pattern. You'll also find out what static and public have meant in the classes you've been filling in. Then you'll build a recipe scaler from nothing but its method calls.
intro.speechText: Good code is mostly small methods with clear names, each doing one job you can test on its own. You'll write your own, with parameters, return values, optional parameters, overloads, and the out parameters behind the TryParse pattern. You'll also find out what static and public have meant in the classes you've been filling in. Then you'll build a recipe scaler from nothing but its method calls.

recap.displayText: The scaler handles every serving size and turns away bad input cleanly. The gotcha: a method that receives a List gets the same list, not a copy, so changing it changes the caller's list too. Next, you'll write classes of your own, with properties and constructors.
recap.speechText: The scaler handles every serving size and turns away bad input cleanly. The gotcha is that a method that receives a List gets the same list, not a copy, so changing it changes the caller's list too. Next, you'll write classes of your own, with properties and constructors.

intro.displayText: A class is a blueprint, and you can build as many things from it as you like. Your mission: finish the blueprint for a Grove pet that you can name, feed and check on.
intro.speechText: A class is a blueprint, and you can build as many things from it as you like. Your mission is to finish the blueprint for a Grove pet that you can name, feed and check on.

recap.displayText: Your pet remembers its name and gets less hungry every time you feed it! Your new word is object: one thing built from a class, with its own values.
recap.speechText: Your pet remembers its name and gets less hungry every time you feed it! Your new word is object, which means one thing built from a class, with its own values.

intro.displayText: Classes are how real C# code models the world: accounts, orders, players, sensors. A good class guards its own rules, so the rest of the program can't put it into a broken state. You'll learn properties, constructors, access modifiers and how objects are shared by reference. Then you'll take a bank account with no rules at all and make it trustworthy.
intro.speechText: Classes are how real C sharp code models the world, like accounts, orders, players and sensors. A good class guards its own rules, so the rest of the program can't put it into a broken state. You'll learn properties, constructors, access modifiers and how objects are shared by reference. Then you'll take a bank account with no rules at all and make it trustworthy.

recap.displayText: The account guards its balance now: no overdrafts, no bad amounts, and no outside code quietly changing it. The gotcha: assigning an object to another variable copies the reference, not the object, so both variables change the same account. Next, you'll put the whole course together in a project.
recap.speechText: The account guards its balance now, with no overdrafts, no bad amounts, and no outside code quietly changing it. The gotcha is that assigning an object to another variable copies the reference, not the object, so both variables change the same account. Next, you'll put the whole course together in a project.

intro.displayText: Time for an adventure that uses everything you've learned: variables, choices, loops, methods and classes. Your mission: guide Pixel along the Grove path, collect treasure and go shopping.
intro.speechText: Time for an adventure that uses everything you've learned, like variables, choices, loops, methods and classes. Your mission is to guide Pixel along the Grove path, collect treasure and go shopping.

recap.displayText: You finished Grove Quest, and the whole C# Basics course! Your new word is project: a bigger program that uses lots of skills together.
recap.speechText: You finished Grove Quest, and the whole C sharp Basics course! Your new word is project, a bigger program that uses lots of skills together.

intro.displayText: This project is shaped like real code: one class per file, a model that guards its own rules, and a class that manages a collection of them. You'll meet two tools you'll use constantly: Dictionary for fast lookups by key, and LINQ for querying collections. The Item class is done; your job is the Inventory that tracks stock, sales and reports. It's the same kind of class you'll put behind a web API later in the track.
intro.speechText: This project is shaped like real code, with one class per file, a model that guards its own rules, and a class that manages a collection of them. You'll meet two tools you'll use constantly, Dictionary for fast lookups by key, and link for querying collections. The Item class is done, and your job is the Inventory that tracks stock, sales and reports. It's the same kind of class you'll put behind a web API later in the track.

recap.displayText: The inventory tracks stock, refuses duplicate SKUs and reports exactly what's running low. That completes C# Basics. The gotcha: indexing a dictionary with a missing key throws, so use TryGetValue or ContainsKey when a key might not be there. Next comes a course on C# objects, then SQL.
recap.speechText: The inventory tracks stock, refuses duplicate stock codes and reports exactly what's running low. That completes C sharp Basics. The gotcha is that indexing a dictionary with a missing key throws, so use TryGetValue or ContainsKey when a key might not be there. Next comes a course on C sharp objects, then sequel.
